newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany recalls success of Erhard economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Germany recalls success of Erhard economic policy.

text.p: Germany takes a nostalgic look back to its postwar roots on Wednesday when Chancellor Helmut Kohl and other leaders ask whether the father of the 1950s "economic miracle" has any answers for the problems of today.

The far-sighted policies of Ludwig Erhard, founder of the "social market economy" underpinning Bonn's democratic rebirth from the ashes of the Third Reich, will be the focus of a day's worth of speeches and discussions among decision-makers now faced with the daunting challenge of a global economy.

Erhard, who would have been 100 years old on February 4, became a legend here by introducing the deutschemark in 1948, liberalising West Germany's shattered economy and creating a "capitalism with a social conscience".

This efficient welfare state, with its consensus between management and labour, and safety net to soften the market's blows, made West Germany relatively immune to the aggressive free market policies pursued in Britain and the United States in the 1980s. Kohl proudly says he is "no Thatcherite".

But this once-lean model has grown fat over the years. Germany's 1990 reunification has strained the machine Erhard built and exposed it to fierce competition from poorer states far less inclined to pamper their workers.

Politicians and businessmen will want to hear how Kohl, who is now caught in a messy effort to balance competing interests while downsizing the welfare state, applies the lessons of his economic mentor to the problems Germany faces.

"This will be a good opportunity in the present debate to make clear what the fundamentals of German economic policy are," a senior Bonn official, who asked not to be named, said of the day of discussions a week ahead of Erhard's anniversary.
"Erhard would not have complained about globalisation or tried to protect the economy. He would have seen it as a chance to modernise and fling open the windows to the winds of change."
Kohl is not expected to announce any policy measures in his speech to over 1,000 guests at the glittering commemoration.

The discussion could get more specific in the afternoon, though, when Finance Minister Theo Waigel leads a discussion about Erhard's legacy with Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt and former finance minister Gerhard Stoltenberg.
Tietmeyer has already been speaking on the issue, telling audiences that Erhard's vision is still very relevant today.
"Globalisation does not attack the concept of the social market economy, only the abuses made in the name of social policy that lead to inflexibility," he said earlier this month.

Tietmeyer was sure the "father of the deutschemark" would support Europe's planned single currency, but only under the strict conditions Bonn demands to ensure that inflation -- the nightmare of German economic policy-makers -- is controlled.
"Stable money and the social market economy are not dusty models from the 1950s," he said. "They are the challenges of the future in the global economy of tomorrow."
The Bundesbank president even found support in Erhard's thoughts for starting the EU's economic and monetary union (EMU) with only a small group of economically fit states.
"I'm sure Erhard would have had no time for the idea that the bigger and more comprehensive a currency area is, the better it must be," he argued.
Erhard, who spent the Nazi years quietly doing economic research in Nuremberg, was put in charge of economic policy in West Germany even before the rump state was founded.

He served as Bonn's first economics minister from 1949 to 1963, the boom period that brought the West Germans unparalleled affluence and helped establish their new democracy as a system with wide popular appeal and support.

Erhard, a portly cigar smoker who distilled his thoughts in a book called "Prosperity for All", succeeded Konrad Adenauer as Bonn's second chancellor in 1963. But he had far less success in the top job and his coalition collapsed in 1966.
The Christian Democrat, who died in 1977, now ranks as one of Germany's postwar visionaries. If pragmatic Bonn has an ideology, the social market economy is it.
Kohl, who likes to portray himself as the political heir to Adenauer, never fails to present his economic policies as the continuation of Erhard's steady path.
To underline this, his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has pasted up posters outside party headquarters with two large photos of Kohl -- one with Adenauer and the other with Erhard.
